title: Fission, fusion and stars
summary: Nuclear fission, chain reactions and reactor design; fusion as the energy source of stars, stellar equilibrium, parallax, luminosity and brightness, the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and stellar evolution.

keyterms.definition: Splitting of a heavy nucleus, usually after neutron absorption, into two smaller nuclei plus neutrons and energy.
Self-sustaining fission in which neutrons released by one fission cause further fissions.
Minimum mass of fissile material needed to sustain a chain reaction.
Material (e.g. water, graphite) that slows fast neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission.
Neutron-absorbing rods (e.g. boron) moved in or out to control the reaction rate.
Joining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy; needs very high temperature to overcome repulsion.
Balance between inward gravity and outward radiation and gas pressure in a stable star.
Total power emitted by a star, L = σAT⁴.
Power received per unit area at the observer: b = L/4πd².
Apparent shift of a nearby star against distant stars; d (parsec) = 1/p (arcsecond).
Plot of luminosity against surface temperature (decreasing to the right) showing star types.
Band on the HR diagram where stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.
Small, hot, dim remnant core of a low-mass star, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.

questions.prompt: What starts the fission of a uranium-235 nucleus in a reactor?
questions.explanation: U-235 captures a thermal neutron, becomes unstable U-236 and splits.

questions.statement: A moderator absorbs neutrons to slow down the chain reaction.
questions.explanation: The moderator slows neutrons (by collisions) without absorbing them; control rods absorb neutrons.

questions.prompt: Match each reactor component to its function.

pairs.right: Removes thermal energy from the core

questions.explanation: Each reactor component has a distinct job.

questions.text: A chain reaction can be sustained only if the mass of fuel is at least the ___ mass.
questions.explanation: Below critical mass too many neutrons escape through the surface to keep the chain going.

questions.prompt: In a fission event, about 200 MeV is released. Most of this appears as
options: kinetic energy of the fission fragments
questions.explanation: Most of the energy is the KE of the two repelling fragments, which becomes thermal energy in the fuel.

questions.statement: In steady reactor operation, on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another fission.
questions.explanation: Control rods keep the multiplication factor at 1; more would grow exponentially, fewer would die out.

questions.prompt: Why is natural uranium usually enriched before use in reactors?
options: To raise the proportion of fissile U-235
questions.explanation: Natural uranium is about 0.7 % U-235; enrichment raises this to a few percent.

questions.text: Neutrons slow down most efficiently in collisions with nuclei of ___ mass, such as hydrogen in water.
questions.explanation: In elastic collisions, maximum KE transfer occurs between equal masses.

questions.prompt: Which is a major disadvantage of fission power?
options: It emits large amounts of CO₂ while running
It has a very low energy density
questions.explanation: Spent fuel stays hazardous for thousands of years and needs secure storage.

questions.prompt: Order the energy transfers in a nuclear power station.
items: Internal energy of the fuel and coolant
questions.explanation: Apart from the heat source, the process matches a fossil-fuel station.

lessons.title: Fusion and the lives of stars

questions.prompt: Why does fusion require extremely high temperatures?
options: So nuclei move fast enough to overcome electrostatic repulsion
questions.explanation: Nuclei must get close enough for the strong force to act, which needs very high kinetic energies.

questions.statement: A main-sequence star is stable because outward radiation and gas pressure balance gravity.
questions.explanation: This hydrostatic equilibrium keeps the star’s size roughly constant for most of its life.

questions.text: A star with parallax angle 0.25 arcseconds is ___ parsecs away.

questions.prompt: Star X has the same surface temperature as star Y but four times the radius. Its luminosity is
questions.explanation: L = σ4πR²T⁴, so L ∝ R²: 4² = 16.

questions.prompt: Two stars have equal luminosity, but star A is twice as far away as star B. A’s apparent brightness is
questions.explanation: b = L/4πd², so doubling d reduces b by 4.

questions.prompt: Match each star type to its description.

pairs.right: Cool surface, very large and luminous
Remnant of a massive star’s supernova

questions.explanation: Position on the HR diagram reveals a star’s stage of life.

questions.text: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, surface temperature ___ from left to right.
questions.explanation: The temperature axis is reversed: hot blue stars on the left, cool red stars on the right.

questions.statement: A star like the Sun will end its life as a neutron star.
questions.explanation: Low-mass stars become red giants, shed planetary nebulae and leave white dwarfs; only massive stars leave neutron stars or black holes.

questions.prompt: Which nuclear process powers a main-sequence star?
questions.explanation: Main-sequence stars convert hydrogen into helium in their cores (e.g. the proton–proton chain).

questions.prompt: Order the life stages of a Sun-like star.
items: Protostar contracting from a gas cloud
questions.explanation: Its evolution is set mainly by its mass.
